titulo: I have a torn meniscus: do I need surgery?
resumen: When a meniscus tear needs surgery and when it does better without it, depending on age, type of tear and symptoms.
descripcion: Meniscus tear: when surgery is needed and when it is better treated without it, according to the evidence. Dr Julio De la Morena, Madrid.
entradilla: Not every meniscus tear needs surgery. In people over 40, most tears seen on an MRI are degenerative, and studies show that exercise gives results similar to arthroscopy. Surgery is reserved for tears that lock the knee and for some traumatic injuries in young people. Dr Julio De la Morena assesses each case with examination and ultrasound at Hospital Memorial Publio Cordón (Pozuelo de Alarcón, Madrid).
imagen_alt: Dr Julio De la Morena reviews a knee MRI
secciones: Two very different types of tear

The meniscus is a fibrocartilage cushion between the femur and the tibia. It tears in two ways. A traumatic tear happens in a young person after a twist or a fall, often playing football, padel or skiing. A degenerative tear appears from the age of 40 without any clear injury: the meniscus has gradually worn and splits with an everyday movement, such as squatting.

The second type is much more common. It is so common that it is found on MRIs of people who have no knee pain at all. So an MRI report saying "meniscus tear" does not, on its own, mean that tear is the cause of the pain.

Several clinical trials have compared arthroscopy with an exercise programme in middle-aged people with degenerative tears. Results at one, two and five years are similar for pain and function. Some of those trials even compared real arthroscopy with simulated surgery, and found no difference either. Based on these data, clinical guidelines do not recommend operating on a degenerative tear as a first step.

• True locking: the knee gets stuck and will not straighten fully, because a fragment of meniscus has moved.
  • A traumatic tear in a young person, especially if the meniscus can be repaired rather than part of it removed.
  • A tear combined with other injuries, such as an anterior cruciate ligament rupture.
  • Persistent pain despite well-delivered conservative treatment for at least three months, with an examination that clearly points to the meniscus.

Conservative treatment is not waiting. It includes a quadriceps and hip strength programme, adjusting load in sport and daily life, and weight management if needed. When pain stops you progressing, an ultrasound-guided injection can open a window to work in. If there is also osteoarthritis, PRP (platelet-rich plasma) is considered in selected cases.

If you have been offered meniscus surgery, it is worth having someone review the MRI together with an examination and explain how much of the pain really comes from the meniscus. That is what a second opinion does: the aim is not to avoid surgery at all costs, but to have it only when it adds something.
faq: Does a torn meniscus heal by itself?

The meniscus has a poor blood supply and a degenerative tear does not close by itself, but it can stop hurting. Many people regain a functional, pain-free knee with exercise, even though the tear is still visible on the MRI.
Can I play sport with a torn meniscus?

It depends on the type of tear and the symptoms. Many people return to walking, running or padel after a strength programme, adjusting the load. If the knee locks or swells after every effort, it needs to be checked.
What happens if part of the meniscus is removed?
Removing part of the meniscus reduces its ability to absorb shock and, in the long term, can speed up osteoarthritis. That is why, when surgery is done, as much meniscus as possible is preserved.
